e.t: This Hebrew word means “waste.” It describes something being made waste or left in a wasted condition, rather than remaining whole, ordered, or useful. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 24:1 and Nahum 2:10. In both passages it functions as part of a description of devastation or desolation. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is waste and the resulting condition of ruin.

e.t: This word is the proper name “Baal Peor,” identifying the Baal connected with Peor. It refers to a specific named figure rather than describing a general action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 12 times, especially in passages recalling Israel’s involvement with Baal Peor and the consequences that followed. The name is also associated with worship directed toward it and with death in the scriptural record. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “son.” It functions as a noun identifying a male child in relation to a parent or family. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing once in Psalm 2:12 and three times in Proverbs 31:2. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding sentence determines how that family relationship is being presented in each passage.

This Hebrew word means “defiled.” It functions as a description of a person or thing regarded as defiled, rather than naming an action, object, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament data represented here, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 13:29. The word therefore identifies a state or condition; the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is defiled there and why.

Adonikam is a personal name, used to identify a particular person rather than to express a general idea or action. In this Hebrew corpus, it occurs three times: twice in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The available rendering keeps the name as “Adonikam” each time, so the clearest ordinary sense is the name itself. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “rejoicing,” functioning as the thing spoken of when rejoicing is described or associated with an action. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Isaiah: 35:2 and 65:18. SEE connections present it as an object related to giving and creation, showing that rejoicing can be treated as a reality associated with what is given or created. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding text.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses quietness or cessation—“silence” or “rest.” It can describe the absence of sound or activity, and its wording may be rendered in either way depending on the sentence. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalms and Isaiah. Its use in Isaiah 62 is connected with the Lord’s watchful, ongoing concern for Jerusalem, showing that the word can describe a condition that is not to be allowed to continue. The surrounding verse determines whether quietness or rest is most natural.

“Thin” describes something with little thickness or density. It functions as a descriptive word, specifying the physical condition or appearance of a thing rather than naming an action or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs 14 times, including repeated uses in Genesis 41. The same basic description applies wherever the text presents something as lacking thickness. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun and surrounding sentence.

“Zimmah” is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, and the English renderings preserve it as “Zimmah.” Because no ordinary lexical definition is provided for this name, its significance is chiefly its role as the name of a person in the genealogical and historical records where it occurs.

This Hebrew verb means “embrace”: to hold someone closely, usually expressing affection, welcome, or intimate closeness. It describes a physical action, but Scripture also uses it in broader statements about embracing something or someone. The word occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including accounts of people welcoming or holding one another and passages that speak of an appropriate time to embrace. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “Girded,” describing a person or object in a state of being girded. It functions as a descriptive term rather than naming an action by itself. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Proverbs 31:24 and Ezekiel 23:15. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a description of being girded or prepared in that condition.

Hadrach is a proper name rendered “Hadrach,” used to identify a specific entity rather than to express a general quality or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 9:1. Because no explicit definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself is the clearest supported meaning; its precise referent is determined by the passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “vision” or something “notable.” It can describe what is seen in a prophetic revelation, and it can also identify something that stands out as remarkable or prominent. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Isaiah and Daniel. Its use therefore reaches beyond one narrow setting: it may point either to a revealed sight or to an outstanding feature. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

The Hebrew word means “live.” It functions as a verb, describing the condition or action of living rather than naming a person, place, or object. In this Hebrew corpus, it appears six times, all in Daniel, from Daniel 2:4 through Daniel 6:21. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains “live”: it speaks of life continuing or being present.

Hemdan is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Hemdan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or instruction. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Genesis 36:26. Because it appears as a name and no explanatory definition is provided, its ordinary lexical role is simply to identify Hemdan. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s place in the passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a Hittite person or to the Hittite people. It functions as a designation for an ethnic group encountered throughout the Old Testament, including in accounts involving the land, its inhabitants, and Israel’s history. The word occurs 48 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Ezekiel. Its ordinary sense is therefore a people-name: “Hittite.”

The word means “Joseph”: it is a personal name used to identify a particular person, rather than a general description or action. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Psalm 81:5. The English rendering is “Joseph,” and no broader ordinary meaning is established for this occurrence. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew noun refers to "princes": prominent officials serving within a kingdom’s governing structure. It identifies people who hold authority under a king and participate in the administration of the realm. In Daniel, the word is used for officials associated with the Babylonian and Persian governments, including groups presented before the king. It occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, so its meaning is closely connected with royal administration and leadership rather than ordinary people.

This Hebrew word describes something “greenish,” identifying a color or appearance. It is used three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, twice in Leviticus and once in Psalms. Its uses include descriptions associated with visible color, but the surrounding verse determines exactly what object or scene is being described. The word therefore points to a green-tinged appearance rather than expressing an action, person, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word means “where,” referring to a place or asking about a location. It functions as a place-focused question or reference rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 6:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical role is to direct attention to location.

e.t: Chelub is a personal name, rendered “Chelub.” It identifies a person in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than expressing a general idea or action. The name appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: once in a genealogy and once in a list concerning Israel’s appointed officials. Thus, its ordinary function is to identify an individual within Israel’s family and community records, while the surrounding passage determines which Chelub is intended.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “crimson,” a deep red color term. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in 2 Chronicles, and each occurrence is rendered “crimson.” It serves as the color designation for something mentioned in those passages, rather than expressing an action or command. Its exact significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This Hebrew verb means “burned.” It describes burning as an action or condition, whether referring to something that burns or something set ablaze. In the Old Testament, it is used eleven times across eleven verses, including poetic descriptions involving fire and intense heat. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains burning or being consumed by fire.

e.t: This word is the place name “Lachish,” referring to a city in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a description or action. The name appears 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Joshua, Kings, and Chronicles. Scripture presents Lachish in accounts involving its capture, royal dealings, speech against it, and later judgment. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word is preserved as “Ucal,” appearing to function as a proper name rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Proverbs 30:1. Because no short definition or broader usage is available here, “Ucal” is the clearest supported rendering. Its precise identification and role depend on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

e.t: “Maher” functions as a personal name in the Hebrew text. It is concentrated in Isaiah 8:1 and 8:3, where it appears as part of a named identity rather than as a commonly repeated descriptive word. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all within those two verses. Its connection with a birth or begetting theme further supports its use in naming a person. The precise significance of the name in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Mahalath is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Mahalath” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Genesis 28:9 and once in 2 Chronicles 11:18. Its role is therefore to identify a person, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or describe an action, quality, or object.

e.t: Michaiah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Michaiah” in the available English rendering. It identifies people mentioned in four Old Testament verses: 2 Kings 22:12, Nehemiah 12:35, Nehemiah 12:41, and Jeremiah 26:18. As a name, it does not describe an action or quality by itself; its specific reference depends on the person named in each passage. The name appears in speech and command-related settings, but those settings belong to the surrounding verses rather than to the name’s basic meaning.

This Hebrew word is the proper name “Maon,” used as a place name and, in one setting, for people associated with that place. It appears eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including references to Maon in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. In Judges, the related people are called Maonites. The word therefore functions primarily as a geographical or people-designating name rather than as a general description or action.

The Hebrew word Elishua is a personal name, rendered “Elishua.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, in 2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 14:5. Since it is preserved as a name rather than translated into a descriptive English term, its ordinary use is to identify Elishua, not to express a general idea.

The Hebrew word means “gall,” referring to a substance associated with the body. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Job 16:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be explained from the word alone. Its basic lexical sense is gall, while the surrounding context determines how Job’s words use that term.

This Hebrew word means “soul,” functioning as a noun that refers to the soul of a person. It occurs once in the Hebrew corpus, at Job 30:15. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included, its ordinary lexical sense is clearer than any verse-specific emphasis: it identifies the soul rather than an action or event. Its meaning should therefore be read as a personal noun within the sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to “wiles”: deliberate, crafty methods used to gain an advantage over someone. It names deceptive action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 25:18. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context.

This Hebrew word refers to an ant, a small creature known in Proverbs for its purposeful activity. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Proverbs: once in Proverbs 6:6 and once in Proverbs 30:25. The singular rendering is “ant,” while the plural rendering is “ants.” In Proverbs, the word serves as the object of statements directing attention toward these creatures, so its basic meaning is the creature itself rather than an abstract quality or action.

This Hebrew word refers to a “buckler,” a protective piece of defensive equipment. It functions as a noun naming something associated with protection and security. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Psalm 91:4. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning identifies a buckler rather than an action, quality, or person.

This Hebrew verb describes being “tossed.” It can express movement or a disturbed condition, whether referring to something physically thrown about or to people who are unsettled. The word occurs seven times in the Old Testament, including uses rendered “tossed” in Isaiah 54:11 and elsewhere connected with trouble, storm-like movement, or forceful action. Its exact sense in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject.

This Hebrew word refers to a ferry, a means of carrying people across a body of water. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in 2 Samuel. As a noun, it names the crossing vessel or service itself rather than the act of crossing. Its use is connected with transporting people across water, giving the word a practical, concrete sense. The precise details of each occurrence depend on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a swallow, a bird named in two Old Testament passages. Its clearest recorded meaning is “swallow.” The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible, once in Isaiah 38:14 and once in Jeremiah 8:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s particular force in either passage must be understood from its immediate context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “ornaments,” visible items associated with personal decoration. It is used for things that may be put on, removed, or given, and it commonly functions as the object being handled or discussed. The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its clearest recurring sense centered on ornaments rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “deep.” It describes something characterized by great depth, whether understood in a physical or figurative sense. Its basic function is to identify depth rather than an action, person, or object by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:22. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains depth.

This Hebrew verb means “answered”: it describes what someone does when giving a reply to another person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 32 times, mostly in Daniel, with two occurrences in Psalms. In Daniel 2, the word repeatedly marks spoken responses within an exchange. Its basic force is verbal: it identifies the act of answering rather than a person, place, or object.

This Hebrew word means “bare.” It expresses an action in which something is made bare or left without covering. Its uses belong to the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, where it occurs 15 times in 14 verses. The word can describe a person or thing being brought into a bare state, so its exact force depends on what is being made bare in the sentence. It is not itself a noun or a name, but an action word.

This Hebrew verb means “set.” It describes the action of putting something into an intended place or arrangement. Scripture uses it for arranging people or objects, preparing an offering, ordering a lamp, and making an assessment. It occurs 76 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad use for deliberate placement or ordering rather than a single narrow situation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being set and the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “thick.” It functions as a descriptive word, telling the reader that something has substantial thickness rather than naming a person, object, or action. Across its 15 Old Testament occurrences, it is associated with something that covers or obscures, including references connected with the heavens. The surrounding sentence determines what is thick in each passage, but the central idea remains thickness.

This Hebrew word means “the,” functioning as a definite article that points to a particular person, thing, or feature rather than speaking in a general way. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel 5. Its basic role is small but important: it helps identify what is being mentioned as definite or already distinguished in the sentence. The surrounding verse determines exactly what it identifies in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “interpretation.” It refers to the explanation or disclosed meaning of something that requires understanding, especially a matter presented in speech or a message. In Daniel, it is repeatedly connected with making an interpretation known, showing that the word concerns the meaning drawn out from what has been said or revealed. It occurs 32 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all within Daniel, so its normal biblical use is closely associated with interpreting significant words, dreams, or visions.

This Hebrew word means “swell,” describing something becoming enlarged or distended. It functions as an action word, expressing the process of swelling rather than naming an object. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 5:22 and 5:27. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the enlargement or distension of something. The same meaning appears consistently in the available English renderings.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a named place called “Abel.” It functions as a place-name rather than as a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both instances in Genesis 50:11, so its meaning is limited and specific rather than a broad term used throughout Scripture. The surrounding verse determines the full significance of that place name.

Hazelelponi is a personal name referring to an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:3, and is rendered “Hazelelponi.” Because it appears only as a person’s name and no broader definition is given, its ordinary use is simply to identify that individual. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in that genealogy.

This Hebrew word means “joined.” It describes things that are connected together rather than standing separately. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 46:22. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be determined from context. Its single recorded English rendering is “joined,” supporting this basic sense without requiring broader alternatives.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “end.” It functions as a noun identifying the endpoint of a thing, place, period, or extent. It can point to where something finishes or to the outer limit of an area. The word occurs 97 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing broad use for describing boundaries and final points rather than one narrow kind of ending. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to “wrath,” describing a forceful expression of anger. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Ezra 7:23. As a noun, it names the state or expression of wrath rather than describing an action by itself. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic meaning is the presence or display of wrath.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Reaiah.” It identifies individuals in Old Testament genealogical and family records rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Its role in these passages is to identify a person within a recorded lineage or community list.

This Hebrew verb means “tremble.” It describes the action of trembling and can be used of people or situations within the Old Testament. The word occurs 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, so it expresses a recurring scriptural action rather than a rare or isolated idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Arioch is a personal name, not a descriptive word with an English meaning supplied here. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name appears seven times in six Hebrew Old Testament verses, twice in Genesis and five times in Daniel. It is consistently rendered “Arioch.” Its precise role in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “dead,” naming the realm associated with those who have died. Across its 66 Old Testament occurrences, it appears in statements about people descending to it, being brought into it, or being delivered from it. Its use is closely connected with death and with God’s power over life and death. The precise force of the word in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “seven”. It can also express “times” when describing how often something happens, so its sense may be seven repetitions rather than merely the number itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs six times, including uses in Genesis, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. The word appears in statements about measured repetition and quantity, including Genesis 4:15, Psalm 12:6, and Isaiah 30:26. e.t: This Hebrew noun means “foxes,” referring to the small wild animals known by that name. It is used seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including both singular and plural English renderings, so it can identify one animal or more than one according to the sentence. The word appears in passages across Judges, Nehemiah, Psalms, Song of Solomon, Lamentations, and Ezekiel. Its central meaning remains the animal itself; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about it.

Shavsha is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its English rendering is consistently “Shavsha.” Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it tells the reader who a person is in the biblical record, while the surrounding verse supplies that person’s role and significance. The name occurs in 1 Chronicles 18:16.

e.t: Shechem is the name of a place in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is used as a location name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or person. The name appears 63 times in this Hebrew corpus, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Hosea. Its repeated use connects it with places where people travel, live, speak, and gather. The ordinary English rendering is “Shechem.”

Shemiramoth is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in four verses: three occurrences in 1 Chronicles and two in 2 Chronicles. The name is consistently rendered “Shemiramoth,” so its precise significance is not given as a translated meaning in these passages. Its role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Shepham is a Hebrew proper name rendered “Shepham.” It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or person’s character. This word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 34:10–11. Because no broader definition or alternative meaning is given, its clearest sense is the name Shepham itself. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the specific role of this place in the boundary description.

This Hebrew verb means “weighed.” It describes the act of determining weight, especially when measuring something valuable. In the Old Testament, it can also serve in statements involving payment or an amount being accounted for, since weighing was a way to establish value. The word occurs 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, including accounts of weighing money, precious materials, or another measured amount. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to “destruction,” describing a state or result in which something is ruined or brought down. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Chronicles 22:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains destruction. The word therefore points to the destructive outcome being described rather than naming a person, object, or action apart from that outcome.

This word means “signs.” It is a plural noun referring to signs rather than to an action or a person. In its Hebrew Old Testament usage, it appears three times, all in Daniel: twice in Daniel 4 and once in Daniel 6. The available occurrences consistently render it as “signs,” so that is the clearest ordinary meaning. Its precise significance in any one verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “nine,” the number that comes after eight and before ten. It is used as a numeral when stating a quantity, age, measurement, or other count. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 58 times, appearing in passages that count years, people, and other amounts. Its basic meaning remains precise and numerical; the surrounding sentence determines what is being counted. This word is therefore best understood as a straightforward reference to the number nine rather than as a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “fine,” describing a high-quality material or fabric. It is used in the Old Testament in descriptions of clothing, furnishings, and valuable goods, so the word points to excellence or fineness rather than an action. It occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages concerning the tabernacle, temple worship, royal settings, and commerce. Its exact sense in any particular sentence depends on the material or object being described.
